title: Infrastructure pillars
prompt_markdown: Which set contains the three infrastructure pillars introduced in the lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: Deployment, testing, and monitoring

options.label: B
options.text: Compute, storage, and network

options.label: C
options.text: Development, testing, and production

options.label: D
options.text: Applications, users, and source code

grader_markdown: Compute executes workloads, storage retains data, and networking connects resources. The alternatives describe activities, environments, or application-level concerns rather than the three infrastructure pillars.

title: Declarative configuration
prompt_markdown: Which statement best describes a declarative infrastructure definition?

options.label: A
options.text: It records every command an administrator previously executed.

options.label: B
options.text: It specifies the exact sequence of operations for every starting state.

options.label: C
options.text: It describes the desired state, while automation determines how to reach it.

options.label: D
options.text: It guarantees that every operation can run in parallel.

grader_markdown: A declarative definition expresses the intended state. Automation determines the operations needed from the declaration and actual state. Declarative syntax alone does not remove dependencies or guarantee parallel execution.

title: Idempotence
prompt_markdown: An automation run has successfully reached the desired state. Its inputs and the relevant external state then remain unchanged. What should a second idempotent run do?

options.label: A
options.text: Leave the managed state unchanged because it already satisfies the declaration.

options.label: B
options.text: Recreate all resources to prove they can be recreated.

options.label: C
options.text: Skip checking the current state and report success.

options.label: D
options.text: Add another copy of each declared resource.

grader_markdown: Once the desired state is satisfied, repeating an idempotent operation under unchanged relevant conditions should cause no further managed-state changes. Checking the current state is compatible with idempotence; doing nothing without checking does not establish correctness.

title: Cloud service models
prompt_markdown: A team moves from managing virtual machines under IaaS to a managed application platform under PaaS. Which responsibility would typically move towards the provider?

options.label: A
options.text: Deciding the application's business requirements

options.label: B
options.text: Maintaining the team's application source code

options.label: C
options.text: Choosing which application features to release

options.label: D
options.text: Maintaining more of the underlying operating system and runtime platform

grader_markdown: PaaS typically transfers more operating-system and runtime-platform maintenance to the provider. The exact boundary depends on the service. The application team still owns its business requirements and application code.

title: Version-controlled infrastructure definitions
prompt_markdown: Give two benefits of version-controlling infrastructure definitions beyond simply having a backup copy. Explain how each benefit helps a team deliver changes reliably.
grader_markdown:
Award **1 mark each** for two distinct benefits explained in relation to reliable delivery, such as a reviewable change history, peer review before application, automated validation of proposed changes, or a shared record of intended configuration that reduces undocumented edits.

Do not award a separate benefit for merely keeping another copy. A prior definition can support investigation or recovery planning, but reverting a source revision does not automatically restore deleted data or guarantee safe infrastructure rollback.

title: Configuration drift
prompt_markdown: Two servers were created from the same definition. An administrator later changes a managed setting manually on only one server. Explain what configuration drift means in this situation and describe one way to detect or reconcile it.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Actual managed configuration has diverged from the declared or intended state; the manual edit creates a difference from the baseline.
- **1 mark:** A sound detection or reconciliation method: compare actual state with the declaration, investigate the difference, and either restore the approved state or review and record a legitimate change before applying it consistently.

title: Mutable and immutable infrastructure
prompt_markdown: A server needs a new operating-system configuration. Contrast an in-place mutable update with an immutable replacement. Explain what must happen to persistent application data when using the replacement approach.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** A mutable update modifies the existing server; an immutable update replaces it with one prepared from the updated definition or image.
- **1 mark:** Preserve persistent data separately or use a tested migration/backup/restore process before retiring the old server. Replacement must not discard the only copy of application data.

title: Separating infrastructure and server configuration
prompt_markdown: A deployment needs networks and virtual machines, as well as software and service configuration inside those machines. Explain the distinction between these two responsibilities and one benefit of keeping their definitions organized separately.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Infrastructure definitions establish resources and connectivity; server configuration establishes software, files, and service state within those resources.
- **1 mark:** A justified benefit of separating these concerns, such as clearer ownership, reuse of configuration across different resource layouts, focused review, or separate validation of different change types.

Do not require separate repositories or separate products. Separation can exist within a single codebase with a clear interface between responsibilities.

title: Dependencies and changing resource information
prompt_markdown:
An application server needs a network before it can be created. A later configuration step needs the server's assigned address. A team records that address manually in several places. Replacing the server may change the address.

1. Explain the dependency order and which resource information should pass between stages. Why is arranging files in a particular order not enough to express these relationships reliably? **(2 marks)**
2. Propose a way to keep dependent configuration consistent when a server is replaced. Explain why it is preferable to maintaining several handwritten copies of the address. **(2 marks)**
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** The network must exist before the dependent server can be created, and the server's assigned address must be known before the dependent configuration step can use it.
- **1 mark:** Dependencies and required outputs should be explicitly represented; file ordering alone does not describe or maintain the resource relationships reliably.
- **1 mark:** Have the authoritative resource information supply the dependent configuration, and refresh that information when the server is replaced.
- **1 mark:** This avoids independently maintained copies becoming stale or inconsistent and reduces the chance of configuring the wrong machine.

Accept generated configuration, a maintained inventory fed by resource outputs, or another clearly explained way of resolving current information. Do not require a particular dependency syntax or product.

title: Shared definitions and environment differences
prompt_markdown:
Development and production started from copied infrastructure definitions. They are intended to share the same application structure, but production needs greater capacity. After several independent edits, nobody knows whether other differences are intentional.

1. Propose how to organize the shared definitions and environment-specific values. Explain which differences should remain explicit. **(2 marks)**
2. Explain how the team could discover accidental differences and keep future changes reviewable while still allowing the legitimate capacity difference. **(2 marks)**
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Keep the common application structure in a shared, reusable definition rather than independently editing full copies.
- **1 mark:** Keep legitimate environment values, including capacity, explicit and associated with the intended environment. Shared structure need not imply identical values everywhere.
- **1 mark:** Compare existing definitions and actual state against the intended baseline and documented exceptions to identify accidental differences.
- **1 mark:** Review and version shared changes and environment values, validating their effects in the relevant environments before applying them.

Accept different folder or repository layouts if they preserve a clear shared definition and explicit differences. Do not require a particular layout or insist that all differences are drift.

title: Image and running machine
prompt_markdown: What is the relationship between a machine image and a virtual machine?

options.label: A
options.text: The image is the live machine's current CPU and memory usage.

options.label: B
options.text: One image can initialize multiple VM instances, which can later develop different state.

options.label: C
options.text: Every image can initialize only one VM.

options.label: D
options.text: Launching a VM automatically updates the source image whenever the VM changes.

grader_markdown: An image provides the starting state for multiple instances. The instances can change independently after launch; those changes do not automatically rewrite the image.

title: Image building and deployment
prompt_markdown: What distinguishes building a machine image from deploying machines based on that image?

options.label: A
options.text: Building an image automatically replaces every running machine.

options.label: B
options.text: Deployment modifies the shared source image whenever an instance changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Building an image removes the need for any instance-specific configuration.

options.label: D
options.text: Building creates a reusable starting artifact; deployment creates running instances from it.

grader_markdown: Image building prepares a reusable artifact. Deployment uses that artifact to create running instances. Producing a new image does not automatically update existing machines or eliminate instance-specific initialization.

title: Rebuildability
prompt_markdown: The lecture describes a problematic form of a "golden image." What makes that example an anti-pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: The image was modified manually and cannot be reliably recreated from a maintained build definition.

options.label: B
options.text: The organization uses a shared base image.

options.label: C
options.text: The image has been tested before use.

options.label: D
options.text: The image is generated by an automated build pipeline.

grader_markdown: The problem is hidden manual changes and the lack of a maintained, repeatable creation process. A shared baseline or an automated, rebuildable image is not inherently an anti-pattern, even if the team calls it a golden image.

title: Image compatibility
prompt_markdown: A team wants to use the same machine baseline on two virtualization platforms and on different processor architectures. Which assumption is sound?

options.label: A
options.text: Any machine image can boot unchanged on every platform and processor architecture.

options.label: B
options.text: Matching the application's name guarantees that its machine image is compatible.

options.label: C
options.text: The team must check platform and architecture compatibility and may need separate image variants.

options.label: D
options.text: Only disk size determines whether the image can boot.

grader_markdown: Machine images must be compatible with the destination platform and processor architecture. A common intended baseline can require different artifacts or formats for different targets; the exact requirements depend on the target platforms.

title: Stock and custom images
prompt_markdown: Explain the difference between a stock image and a custom image. Give one reason an organization would maintain a custom image instead of configuring every new machine entirely from a stock image at launch time.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** A stock image is a supplied starting image; a custom image adds selected organizational software or configuration to a starting image.
- **1 mark:** A sound reason, such as a consistent security baseline, less repeated installation, faster initialization, or a tested common starting state.

title: Build time and boot time
prompt_markdown: Explain how configuration prepared during image building differs from configuration applied when an instance first starts. Give one suitable example for each stage.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Build-time configuration becomes part of a reusable image, for example common software or a shared security baseline.
- **1 mark:** Boot-time initialization configures a particular instance when it starts, for example its environment-specific settings or instance identity.

Accept different placements if the distinction and trade-off are sound. First-start initialization is not automatically ongoing state reconciliation.

title: Containers and virtual machines
prompt_markdown: Explain one important difference between a typical Linux container and a virtual machine in how they use the operating-system kernel. State one practical consequence for their isolation or compatibility.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Typical Linux containers share a host kernel; virtual machines run a guest operating system with its own kernel over virtualized hardware.
- **1 mark:** A valid consequence for isolation or compatibility, such as sharing a kernel-level boundary, needing a compatible host kernel, or being able to run a different guest kernel in a VM.

Do not accept claims that containers have no isolation or that any image runs unchanged on any operating system and processor architecture.

title: Snapshot and rebuildable definition
prompt_markdown: A team keeps a snapshot of a working server but has no maintained instructions for recreating its configuration. Explain one thing the snapshot provides and one reason it does not replace a rebuildable definition.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** A snapshot captures a point-in-time state that may help restore or clone a machine, subject to its scope and consistency.
- **1 mark:** It does not explain or maintain the intended construction process; hidden configuration and manual changes remain difficult to review, modify, and recreate deliberately. A maintained build definition makes those inputs and steps explicit.

Do not imply snapshots are useless or that definitions replace backups of persistent data.

title: Organizing an image family
prompt_markdown:
A company needs web-server and database-server images. Both must share a security baseline, but each needs different software. Today, two separate build definitions contain copied baseline steps. A policy update was applied to only one copy.

1. Propose an organization for the image definitions that separates shared baseline work from workload-specific work. Explain how it reduces the risk illustrated here. **(2 marks)**
2. Explain what must happen to the derived images and running machines after the shared baseline changes. Include a check before the new baseline is used in production. **(2 marks)**
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Define a common baseline once and build separate workload-specific images from it, or reuse an equivalent common build unit in both image definitions.
- **1 mark:** Central ownership of shared baseline logic reduces duplicated edits and inconsistent policy implementation while keeping workload differences separate.
- **1 mark:** Rebuild the affected derived images and explicitly roll out or replace the running machines; changes to a shared definition do not propagate automatically into existing artifacts or instances.
- **1 mark:** Validate the new baseline and derived workload behavior before production use, such as checking the policy setting and exercising the application on a candidate image.

Accept a dependency diagram or prose. Reuse alone does not prove that a built artifact or running fleet is current.

title: Reproducible builds and immutable updates
prompt_markdown:
An image build always selects the latest available base image and software packages. A team claims: "Our build instructions are version-controlled, so running them next month must produce the same software versions."

1. Assess the claim. Identify two inputs that can change independently of the instructions and explain how to control them when reproducing an approved version. **(2 marks)**
2. The team deliberately prepares a patched image. Describe an immutable update to the running application, including validation and preservation of persistent data. **(2 marks)**
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** The selected base image can change independently of the build instructions; record and select the approved version when reproducing it.
- **1 mark:** Software package versions or their source contents can change; control the approved versions and ensure the required artifacts remain available. Versioned instructions alone do not freeze external inputs.
- **1 mark:** Build and validate the patched image, create replacement instances, check application health, and move the workload to the replacements with a considered recovery path.
- **1 mark:** Preserve persistent data on suitably managed storage or use a tested migration/restore process before retiring old instances.

Do not require a specific package manager, image identifier, or artifact-storage product.

title: Inventory
prompt_markdown: What is the main purpose of an inventory in server configuration management?

options.label: A
options.text: To store a complete binary snapshot of every server

options.label: B
options.text: To replace all reusable configuration definitions

options.label: C
options.text: To identify managed hosts and groups and associate relevant targeting information

options.label: D
options.text: To record only the operations that previously failed

grader_markdown: An inventory identifies target hosts and groups and can associate relevant information with them. It supports selecting the appropriate targets for configuration; it is not a complete backup of their state.

title: Partial state management
prompt_markdown: An automation system manages only the resources explicitly declared to it. Its declaration requires a web service but says nothing about an unrelated package installed manually. What should you expect after a successful run?

options.label: A
options.text: The unrelated package can remain because it is outside the declared scope.

options.label: B
options.text: Every package not named in the declaration is automatically removed.

options.label: C
options.text: The machine is necessarily recreated from a stock image.

options.label: D
options.text: Success proves that every aspect of the machine matches a complete baseline.

grader_markdown: The system in the question manages explicitly declared resources. A resource outside that scope is not automatically declared absent, so unmanaged state can remain even after successful configuration.

title: Reusable configuration units
prompt_markdown: What is the strongest reason to organize server configuration into reusable units for common setup, web services, and databases?

options.label: A
options.text: It guarantees that all configuration actions can run simultaneously.

options.label: B
options.text: It makes each unit independent of every other resource and input.

options.label: C
options.text: It removes the need to test how the units work together.

options.label: D
options.text: It groups related responsibilities so they can be understood, reused, and maintained separately.

grader_markdown: Grouping related responsibilities creates units that can be understood, reused, and maintained. Such units can still have dependencies and need integration testing; splitting files does not guarantee independence or parallelism.

title: Configuration values and shared logic
prompt_markdown: Development and production use the same service configuration logic but need different capacity values. Which organization best supports reuse and makes the intended differences clear?

options.label: A
options.text: Copy the full logic for each environment and edit the copies independently.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep shared logic reusable and supply explicit environment-specific values through a documented configuration scheme.

options.label: C
options.text: Hide the production values inside unrelated shared configuration files.

options.label: D
options.text: Require both environments to have identical capacity so no values differ.

grader_markdown: Shared logic plus explicit environment values preserves reuse and makes intentional differences reviewable. A documented configuration scheme makes the effective values understandable; copying whole definitions or hiding overrides makes divergence harder to control.

title: Grouping by responsibility
prompt_markdown: A fleet contains web, database, and batch-processing servers. All need a common baseline, but their workload-specific configuration differs. Explain how host grouping and reusable configuration units can express both requirements without applying every workload to every server.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Apply a common baseline to the fleet or a shared parent grouping.
- **1 mark:** Apply workload-specific units only to the corresponding web, database, or batch groups. Explain that separating selection from reusable definitions avoids copying the baseline or installing every workload everywhere.

Do not require a particular inventory syntax, directory structure, or naming convention.

title: Desired state and operational actions
prompt_markdown: Explain the difference between declaring that a service should be running and requesting that it restart on every automation run. Why does the distinction matter for repeated execution?
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Declaring a running service describes a condition; requesting a restart describes an operation even when that condition is already satisfied.
- **1 mark:** Reapplying the desired state can leave an already running service undisturbed, while unconditional restarts can cause unnecessary disruption. A restart may still be appropriate when a relevant change requires it.

title: Responding to configuration changes
prompt_markdown: A service must reload to use changed configuration. Explain why it can be useful to reload only after relevant changes, and why several compatible configuration changes might be applied before a single reload.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Change-aware reloads apply necessary configuration changes while avoiding unnecessary disruption when relevant configuration is unchanged.
- **1 mark:** Combining compatible changes before one reload avoids redundant work and lets the service consume a coherent configuration. The changes should be validated and ordered appropriately before activation.

Assess the principle, not a product's notification rules or handler timing.

title: Configuration success and functional success
prompt_markdown: Every configuration step reports success, but users still cannot use the application. Explain why these outcomes are compatible and give one functional check that could reveal a problem missed by configuration-level checks.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Configuration success establishes that selected operations or resource checks succeeded, not that the complete application works for its users.
- **1 mark:** A relevant functional check, such as making a representative application request, confirming database access from the application, or verifying communication between components.

Award credit for explaining the check's purpose; a successful configuration exit status alone is not a functional check.

title: Comparing codebase organizations
prompt_markdown:
A team is choosing between one large configuration file for all server types and environments, and smaller reusable units with a separate place to select which units and values each environment uses.

1. Propose sensible boundaries for the smaller units and explain one advantage over the single large file as the system grows. **(2 marks)**
2. Explain one cost or risk introduced by splitting the configuration, and how you would keep the resulting codebase understandable and safe to change. **(2 marks)**
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Propose coherent units, for example a common baseline plus separate web, database, and batch responsibilities, with a clear place for environment selection and values.
- **1 mark:** Explain a benefit such as focused review, reuse, clearer ownership, or reducing duplicated logic as the system grows.
- **1 mark:** Identify a real cost or risk: more interfaces and indirection, unclear dependencies, conflicting defaults, or excessive fragmentation that makes the effective configuration hard to follow.
- **1 mark:** Address that risk with clear interfaces, documented inputs and override rules, visible composition, sensible unit size, or appropriate integration validation.

A single file can be adequate for a small system. Do not award full credit for claiming that more files are always better, or require one prescribed repository layout.

title: Checking the intended state
prompt_markdown:
A deployment process skips software setup whenever it finds a directory named "application". The directory remains after the desired application version changes. The process reports success without checking the installed version or whether the application works.

1. Explain why this check is insufficient and why an unchanged result does not by itself prove that automation has reached the desired state. **(2 marks)**
2. Propose a better way to decide whether an update is needed, and one check after the update that would provide evidence that the intended result was achieved. **(2 marks)**
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Directory existence does not establish that the intended software version or configuration is present.
- **1 mark:** Repeatedly doing nothing can leave an incorrect state unchanged. Idempotence and convergence to the desired state are related but distinct properties; a no-op alone is not evidence of successful configuration.
- **1 mark:** Compare a meaningful observed state, such as the installed version or artifact identity, with the desired version/configuration and update when they differ. Include handling missing or incomplete installations in a sound explanation.
- **1 mark:** Verify the intended version/configuration or exercise the relevant application behavior after the update. Rechecking directory existence alone is insufficient.

Accept in-place reconciliation or replacement from a verified artifact if the student explains how the intended state is established and checked.
